title: What Democratic Socialists Want
author: Fred Block
content:
![What Democratic Socialists
Want](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-28-at-10.20.14
---PM.png)

> _The Blueprint: How Socialism Can Work in the Real World_  
>  By Mike Beggs, Ben Burgis, and Bhaskar Sunkara  
> Verso, 432 pages, $29.95

The surprising electoral success of avowedly socialist candidates in big-city
mayoral campaigns and some congressional races has raised the profile of the
Democratic Socialists of America, forcing people to ponder what the term
"democratic socialism" actually means. By some accounts, it means a system
along the lines of Scandinavian social democracy: guaranteeing all citizens
access to health care, child care, affordable housing, and support in old age,
while leaving capitalists in charge of their firms. For President Trump and
his allies, conversely, democratic socialism is a euphemism, and its advocates
are communists and jihadists who hate capitalism and want to destroy economic
and political freedom.

Neither answer is accurate. Most leading democratic socialists envision an
eventual transition away from an economy dominated by profit-maximizing firms.
They recognize that in the decades after World War II, the United States and
other nations created a regulated capitalism that limited inequalities of
income and wealth and assured a certain level of prosperity for working-class
people. But the last five decades saw the dismantling of many of these
regulations, allowing the return of vast inequalities of wealth, more economic
insecurity for working people, and the accumulation of ever greater political
power by billionaires.

Democratic socialists believe that radical changes are necessary to undo this
economic and political damage. However, they invoke the aphorism that the
definition of insanity is to repeat the same thing and expect different
results. They insist that another experiment with regulated capitalism will
end with capitalists again using their power to liberate themselves from
higher taxes and new regulations. They believe that the only reliable path to
a more egalitarian society is a series of reforms that eventually eliminate
the control of capitalists over the economy's productive resources. In short,
they favor creating a socialist economy.

> "The Soviet model of state socialism failed economically."

But how would a socialist economy be organized? For all of its defects,
capitalism has dramatically raised the standard of living in Europe, North
America, and other places. Would a socialist economy be similarly dynamic, or
would it bring about a significant decline in living standards? The Soviet
model of state socialism failed economically. The revolt against Soviet
communism began in East Germany, where it was obvious that living standards
were far below those of its West German neighbor. But similar discontent
ultimately doomed the Soviet model across Eastern Europe and Russia.
Meanwhile, China and Vietnam responded to this failure by opening their
economies to private profit-oriented firms.

A new book, _The Blueprint: How Socialism Can Work in the Real World,_ argues
that an economically productive socialism is possible. The book is written by
Mike Beggs, a political economist, Ben Burgis, a philosopher, and Bhaskar
Sunkara, the founding editor of _Jacobin --_the leading socialist publication
in the United States. The authors believe that the path to that productive
socialist economy requires understanding why the Soviet planned economy proved
a failure.
